stories.title: Return Of The Repressed In Germany
stories.summary: The post Return Of The Repressed In Germany appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Identity and the alias nation.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Even if we know it is the way of history, it is nonetheless jarring to witness time and again the return of the repressed in the cultural and political life of nations. It is never over, even after the fat lady sings.

The fat lady sang twice in Germany, first after Nazism was roundly defeated in World War II and second, after the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet bloc collapsed and “history ended.” Only decades later are we seeing an eruption of all that was left unsettled with the steady rise of neo-Nazi parties, mainly in former East Germany, and the demise of the mainstream political coalitions that were the pillars of post-war liberal democracy.

Looking Back To Three Decades Ago

Some three decades ago, New Perspectives Quarterly (NPQ) published an issue focused on the reignited embers of nationalism in Germany. It reads like a chronicle of the future foretelling the tremors shaking Europe’s most powerful country today.

Contributors to that issue ranged from Daniel Cohn-Bendit, the celebrated May ‘68 rabble-rouser and then-Green Party’s deputy mayor of Frankfurt, to the controversial playwright Hans Jürgen Syberberg, who broke post-war taboos with his movie, “Hitler: A Film From Germany.” Other contributors included Germany’s president at the time, Richard von Weizsäcker and then-foreign minister Hans Dietrich Genscher, whose essay was titled “Nationalism Has No Home in Germany.”

Even then, the issues that stirred the most virulent passions were around the influx of immigrants, lenient asylum policies and the “yearning for a lost sense of belonging.” At the time, isolated gangs were firebombing immigrant homes. Today, those sentiments have been channeled into political parties that garner as high as 44% of the vote in regional elections.

The introduction I wrote to that long-ago NPQ edition read: “Now that the long post-war parole is over, will Germany prove to be reformed or a repeat offender? Unable to face itself, Germany for decades assumed an identity for the benefit of others in order to absolve its crimes. It has become an alias nation hiding its soiled soul under the bushel of NATO and the European community, which, above all else, institutionalizes the liberal ideal of a rational order over a national one.”

Citing the filmmaker Syberberg on why the “democratic repression” associated with rational liberalism cannot forever bury the soul, it continued: “If the cool head allows the passions of the soil no expression, then those underground passions will surface in the ugliest form time and again. A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

Syberberg argued that “after the war, intellectuals stood on the tradition of the Enlightenment and a hegemonic rationalism that focused on the head at the expense of the heart. Culture is built upon the way the light falls on the trees, the way the heavens look at night from the familiarity of a particular place where people live and feel a sense of belonging to a unique way of life, to our garden plots, folk tales and Teutonic fantasies.

“Yet we have felt compelled in Germany to repress this uniqueness. We feel safe excelling at mathematics, physics, business. Our people, dominated by facts and figures, are satisfied to dance around the golden calf of materialism and the strong Deutschmark. We are very efficient and methodical. But where is the heart?”

“Heimat,” or homeland, he went on, “was one of the aesthetic subjects that was forbidden territory after the war.” When the Cold War ended and the wall came down, 15 million people became orphans from an East Germany that no longer existed. “They have a strong sense of Heimat precisely because they have lost their homeland,” Syberberg said. “People need food and shelter, but they also need love, community, a home. This is part of the natural function of being human.”

“A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

To the filmmaker, the extremism of gangs bombing the homes of immigrants was “frightening, like wild animals.” But he thought it was not enough to condemn it; he also needed to understand “what it is in the air nourishing it.” For him, it was a “reaction not fully formed” springing from the wound of historical dislocation and the prohibition, both explicit and implicit, against cherishing one’s own identity when strangers were welcomed.

Heiner Müller, the liberal playwright and counterpoint to Syberberg on the German literary scene, offered much the same analysis. He too addressed the dislocation of East Germans after the end of the Cold War. Today, the strongholds of the neo-Nazi parties are in the former East.

“After the death of socialism as epitomized by the GDR, Germany’s new demon has become neo-Nazi extremism,” he said. “This should surprise no one. With the demise of socialism, and then reunification, a vacuum was created. Capitalism no longer had an enemy, which meant it no longer had an alibi when people failed to thrive. In the wake of discredited left-wing ideologies, right-wing extremism has simply assumed the role of capitalism’s harshest critic.”

For Müller, “there can be no dialogue with the neo-Nazis. They are not interested in dialogue. They are merely following their own logic: the logic of the void. And they are filling the void with nationalism. In the 19th century, radicals sought to appease the ‘God is dead’ trauma through socialism. Today, not only is God dead, but utopias have vanished. There are no values left. From this extends freedom — but also longing — to belong, to be part of a group, a community, a nation.

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West,” Müller presciently remarked.

When I spoke in those days to Cohn-Bendit, aka “Danny the Red” of the May ‘68 Paris student uprising, he focused as well on former East Germany, where most of the bombings took place. As he put it, “People in the East unrealistically thought unification would bring their living standards up to the level of the West overnight. But that will take decades. In reality, their life will get worse before it gets better, and so they face a future of fear and uncertainty.

“What happens when you throw 400,000 refugees into that cauldron of angst? The refugees and immigrants present the opportunity to give a name and a face to the fears that plague them. As such, they become a target for aggression. For the recently liberated Easterners, the new freedom from censorship means being able to say, ‘We don’t want foreigners.’”

As deputy mayor of Frankfurt, Cohn-Bendit dealt with the multicultural challenge up close. In those days already, 25% of the population was foreign-born. This experience led him to propose “tightening” German immigration and asylum laws, for which he was, in his words, “greeted with scorn and controversy by the old left, which steadfastly supports open borders at all costs.”

Zooming out to the big picture, he said: “I would like to see a world where no individual is obliged to leave their place of birth to seek safety, opportunity or even the basic necessities of life. Alas, that is not the world we live in. We live in a global society that is highly unequal with respect to chances in life.

“Unless the next 20 years can bring hope to the children of the poor South and East, the run on our borders won’t stop. Germans must adjust to this reality and impose limits but also realize we are already an immigrant society” that democracy must accommodate. Read Noema in print.

President von Weizsäcker wrote that Germans, above all, must respect the dignity of all persons given its past. Yet he acknowledged that the asylum laws were not designed for a “massive influx of foreigners” and that the bottleneck must be broken by a new system “that controls and limits immigration as well as protects the true right of asylum.”

Even as the passions of renewed nationalism stirred at the grassroots, the leadership of Europe was moving in the opposite direction. In NPQ’s forum, foreign minister Genscher said: “The new civilization of coexistence within our European community must never again be jeopardized by national self-interest. We must not only preserve and further develop this new civilization of coexistence for ourselves but extend it to our neighbors in the East. “

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West.”

In this, he was fully in tune with the mindset of the other elders of European integration shaped by the horrors of World War II. At the time, French President François Mitterrand put it bluntly: “Nationalism means war.”

The disconnect that has become so manifest today was set in motion then. The good faith efforts to avoid repeating the past clashed with a lost sense of home and belonging. That nascent alienation has only grown, not diminished, over time.

And all this was compounded two decades later when Chancellor Angela Merkel opened wide the country’s gates to some 900,000 refugees from the Syrian civil war in 2015.

The Elusive Conundrum

The conundrum of how to calibrate the right balance between the human need for belonging and compassion for the peril, struggles and aspirations of the dispossessed trying to make a new life remains elusive — and global. The same issue haunts all of Europe today, the United States and even the developing world, from South Africa to the Bangladesh-India borderlands.

In this context, it is wrong to keep saying that governments which tighten strictures on immigration are “moving to the right.” What is happening is that the ongoing incapacity to find a proportionate balance between host populations and incomers has become a mainstream concern, and democratic systems are only responding as they should.

Lessons From The German Experience And Elsewhere

What lessons can be learned from the German experience and elsewhere?

First, liberals should stop treating every expression of the defense of belonging as somehow resurrecting the ghost of Hitler. “To be human means to belong,” the great pluralist philosopher Isaiah Berlin posited in a conversation we had at the outset of the Balkan wars in the 1990s. “If the streams dry up, where men and women are not products of a culture, where they don’t have kith and kin and feel closer to some people than to others, where there is no native language—that would lead to a tremendous desiccation of everything that is human.”

Second, communities, nations or unions like Europe have an obligation to their citizens to control immigration based on criteria that ensure newcomers will abide by their norms and values and contribute positively to the economic well-being of the given jurisdiction. Societies and cultures are not closed systems, but states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories. The social contract of any polity with its citizens rests on this proposition.

To that end, borders must be secure, not porous. The best formulation of this comes from the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate in Texas, James Talarico. “Our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door,” he has said, so the homeowner decides who to let in.

Absent this enforced conviction, we will see the kind of mean-spirited and cruel crackdowns being practiced in the U.S. today or on the Mediterranean Sea to remedy an out-of-control situation after the fact. Better to prevent that eventuality in the first place. As the French philosopher Régis Debray put it in an apt aphorism: “Borders are a vaccine against the epidemic of walls.”

Third, we need to redefine the concept of asylum for the times we live in. In the mid-20th century, asylum was meant to provide safe refuge for those persecuted by their governments or temporarily fleeing the ravages of war. It was never meant as a path to permanent residency or to offer a haven for the mass exodus of those from states too weak to protect their own citizens or provide them with economic opportunity.

Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states. Bad faith results from good intentions if the capacity to fulfill moral claims is lacking.

The next conundrum on this front will involve climate refugees forced to leave their homeland because of the floods, droughts and famines associated with global warming for which the industrialized nations of the North are historically most responsible.

Fourth, aging societies in the North must shed the illusion that they can live without legal immigration, and that means a more multicultural mix than ever before. Avoiding cultural, security and economic clashes as this new reality takes hold entails proactive policies for assimilation and integration.

“Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states.”

The aim must be to prevent the further formation of the kind of cultural silos of immigrants concentrated in segregated neighborhoods that evolve into economic castes, as already seen for so long in places like the Parisian suburbs. In Sweden, immigrants’ lack of necessary skills and education to compete in the job market has made them among the least integrated in Europe. The gap carries on to the children, who are disproportionately engaged in what have become violent street gangs in that one-time social democratic paradise.

Integration begins with the right immigration criteria. Canada is more successful at integrating immigrants than most because some 60% are admitted through the “economic class,” which counts both assets and skills that match labor market needs. By contrast, according to Harvard University’s Paul May, two-thirds of permanent residents accepted in the U.S are admitted for family reunification, while less than 20% are based on skills.

In areas where borders are contiguous, such as the U.S. and Mexico, and there is great demand for lower-wage employment in agriculture, services and construction, a work permit system that enables easy transit across borders but does not confer permanent residency is a sensible approach. To avoid the exploitative conditions of such prior programs, labor rights conditions need to be monitored and rigorously enforced.

Ongoing integration entails institutions designed for that purpose. In California, the majority of the population today is Latino and Asian, and mostly second generation. Though challenges remain, integration has been largely successful because public higher education serves as a cultural mixer and transmission belt to the middle class. The California State University System has 470,000 students at 23 campuses in every region of the state. Its students, often the first in their families to go to college, match the immigrant profile: 48% are Latinos and 16% are Asian.

Open Societies Need Defined Borders

Open societies need defined borders to sustain a common sense of identity. One is a condition of the other. The lack of either will condemn both to the untenable situation we face today. Among the many challenges of the 21st century, balancing belonging and becoming is the one closest to home.

stories.title: Fifty Billion Seedlings: Can Ethiopia Replant Its Ravaged Forests?
stories.summary: A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world's most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive. stories.body:
Women water seedlings at a nursery near Buee, Ethiopia. Michael Tewelde / AFP via Getty Images

A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world’s most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive.

By Samuel Abate and Freddie Clayton • October 1, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Niku Argane’s farm sits on a steep hillside in central Ethiopia’s semi-mountainous Gurage Zone, where years of flooding have carved deep gullies through the land. Soil that once produced enough barley and potatoes to feed his wife and four children — and left a surplus to sell in the market — has eroded, while drought has made what land remains harder to cultivate.

“We have never stopped farming, but our production declined because of land degradation,” the 32-year-old said from his farm in Ambele Kebele.

Over the last century, Ethiopia nearly eradicated its forests as trees were cleared for farming, grazing, and fuel. The loss of tree cover and tree roots allowed wind and rain to wash away fertile topsoil and contributed to declining crop yields. That vulnerability is now being compounded by climate change. Ethiopia is among the countries most vulnerable to its effects: Heavier downpours are sluicing away depleted soils and triggering landslides, while more intense droughts, combined with the loss of shade that trees once provided, rapidly dry out the land.

Land degradation costs the country an estimated $4.3 billion a year through smaller harvests and lost income to farmers, which also means there is less food to eat. With more than 100 million Ethiopians dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods, the consequences reach far beyond the environment. Climate shocks and crop losses are among the biggest drivers of acute hunger; in 2024, 15.8 million Ethiopians were estimated to need food assistance, roughly 12 percent of the population.

Reforestation almost always fails, says a researcher, but even if 30 percent of trees planted in Ethiopia survive, “it’s still huge.”

Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. In just the last seven years, tens of millions of Ethiopians have planted more than 47 billion seedlings across the country in one of the world’s largest environmental restoration campaigns. Volunteers for the program, which aims to plant 50 billion seedlings by 2030, are planting trees to rebuild native forests and integrating them into farmland. In the process, they are sequestering carbon to help protect future generations from ever more extreme weather.

Such programs often fall short, but Ethiopians are finding hope in the scale of their ambitions. “Reforestation is one of the most difficult things you can imagine,” said Aad Kessler, a researcher at the Netherlands’ Wageningen University. “It almost always fails, but this is so big that even if 30 percent of the trees survive, it’s still huge.”

In the early 20th century, forests covered an estimated 35 to 40 percent of Ethiopia. Its highlands were greener, with forests spanning much of the country’s cool, fertile uplands. But as populations grew and settlements spread, trees were cleared for agriculture, pasture, fuel, and construction. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent , while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

Farms in North Gondar in the Ethiopian highlands. The spread of agriculture has stripped the region of trees. Danita Delimont Creative

After the devastating droughts and famines of the 1970s and 1980s, Ethiopia’s government and international donor organizations began investing heavily in soil and water conservation, excluding livestock from worn-out land, planting trees across the country, and building terraces and check dams — small, low barriers of rocks and logs placed across gullies — to slow the flow of rainwater. By the 2000s, restoration programs were being implemented at increasing scale.

The government supercharged that effort in 2019 by turning tree-planting into a nationwide campaign with a scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative, which mobilized millions of individuals and groups, including farmers, public servants, schools, and religious organizations, and distributed free seedlings across the country. In 2024, the government established the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, committing 0.5 percent to 1 percent of the annual federal budget — roughly $73 million to $145 million — to restoring landscapes. It was an unusually large commitment for a low-income country, and the program’s success and ambition, according to development experts, contributed to the selection of Ethiopia as the host of next year’s U.N. climate conference — a prestigious honor that will help the nation showcase its greening efforts.

You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, says an ecologist, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

In August, 26.6 million Ethiopians planted 800 million tree seedlings in a single day, according to government figures , beating the previous year’s tally of 714.7 million . One of the volunteers, Yeshihareg Teferi, traveled at sunrise from her home in Addis Ababa to Tulu Dimtu so she could hunch in the rain to dig holes in the mud. It was Teferi’s fifth year participating in the annual event. Previously she’d planted indigenous species, including African wild olive and African fern pine. This time, she chose juniper. “We have a responsibility to ensure future generations inherit a green and fertile environment, rather than barren land,” she said.

There are already signs the work is having an impact.

The government reports that national forest cover rose from 17.2 percent in 2019 to 23.6 percent in 2023, while studies of restored areas have found substantial reductions in soil erosion. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from more than 350 square miles to around 100 square miles.

Volunteers plant seedlings on the outskirts of Addis Ababa as part of a nationwide tree-planting drive in early August.

Such efforts can also benefit wildlife. In Abijata-Shalla National Park, in the Ethiopian highlands, workers replanted degraded areas and built terraces and contour bunds (small earthen ridges that run across hillsides to slow runoff and allow water to soak into the soil). As trees and native grasses returned, more water infiltrated into the ground, and water levels on lakes in the park began to rise, said Kumera Wakjira, director-general of the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority. More water spurred the return of fish and fish-eating birds like cormorants and African darters. Grant’s gazelles and wild dogs are also expanding into areas where they were previously scarce, Wakjira said.

But planted trees are not guaranteed to survive. A 2022 study of 176 reforestation projects in Asia found that around half of planted trees did not live five years. And trees alone do not make a forest, said Endalkachew Wolde-Meskel, a soil scientist and senior researcher at the Center for International Forestry Research: That process usually requires the regeneration of grasses and other vegetation, in addition to soil- and water-conservation measures and management by local communities. “The objective is not really ‘plant trees,’” he said. “It is to restore the functioning of the entire landscape.”

Emiru Birhane Hizikias, an Ethiopian restoration ecologist at Norway’s Nord University, said it was a “blessing, politically speaking,” to have the prime minister lead on tree planting but that the scale of the Green Legacy Initiative had outpaced the systems needed to make it work effectively on the ground. Too often, he said, the focus is on getting huge numbers of seedlings into the earth rather than ensuring their survival. You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, he said, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

Climate change has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season.

Abreham Berta Aneseyee, an environmental scientist at Ethiopia’s Wolkite University and an adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture, disputes that characterization, saying the planting campaign is accompanied by practical advice from government experts in forestry and farming. The experts go from farm to farm, advising smallholders on how to plant and care for different types of seedlings, he said, including how deeply to place them in soil and how to conserve soil with structures like bunds. They also advise farmers on managing forests and protecting trees rather than cutting them down.

A 2026 study of more than 44,500 seedlings planted in southern Ethiopia under the Green Legacy Initiative in 2023 found that about 80 percent had survived, with rates significantly higher among older seedlings, wet-season plantings, and seedlings whose planters had received training in best “plantation practices.” In Humbo and Boloso Sore districts in Ethiopia’s southwestern Wolaita Zone, the Green Legacy Initiative has been layered onto longer-running efforts to sustainably manage land, with communities building check dams to stabilize gullies, digging half-moon ditches to trap water and let it soak into the soil, and planting trees alongside grasses and other vegetation.

Left: Half-moon ditches trap runoff, helping to nourish plants and combat erosion. Right: A check dam in a gully stems erosion by slowing the flow of water. Courtesy of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT

Ethiopia’s approach has few direct parallels in Africa for its combination of political leadership, funding, public mobilization, and scale, said Kessler of Wageningen University. He compared the effort with China’s restoration of the Loess Plateau, one of the world’s most highly eroded regions. In the 1990s, China launched major restoration efforts on the plateau, including a World Bank-backed watershed rehabilitation project and, starting in 1999, the Grain for Green program, which paid farmers to restrict cultivation and plant trees, shrubs, and grasses. By 2016, more than 11,500 square miles of rain-fed cropland had been converted to more dense forest or grassland, contributing to a 25 percent increase in vegetative cover in a decade.

The comparison has limits, though. China paid farmers to take degraded slopes out of cultivation, while millions of Ethiopian smallholders still depend on the land for food and livelihoods. But Kessler said the two efforts shared a fundamental approach: “Do it massively, and then see where you end up.”

Kessler’s work, which includes a government-backed field project in Ethiopia, takes a more participatory approach, involving farmers and communities in decisions about what to restore and how. “Of course it is better [than top-down action],” he said, “but it takes more time.”

Even as Ethiopia invests in rebuilding forests and soils, climate change is altering the conditions landscapes must withstand. In the arid pastoral regions of Afar and Somali, the Green Legacy Initiative focuses on drought-tolerant species, but it is unclear whether the trees planted today will be able to withstand the conditions they face decades from now.

Volunteers search for bodies in the aftermath of a 2024 landslide in the Geze Gofa district in southern Ethiopia. Michele Spatari / AFP via Getty Images

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects more frequent and intense rainfall in East Africa as global temperatures rise. In July 2024, exceptionally heavy rainfall in Ethiopia’s Geze Gofa district, in the southern highlands, triggered two landslides that killed at least 257 people. Recent studies also suggest that climate change is making El Niños more frequent and severe, with consequences for East Africa. This summer, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network linked El Niño to “historically poor” summer rains in parts of Ethiopia, leaving some areas with their driest June and July on record.

For some farmers, the changing climate has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season. Belayneh Mamo, 65, a farmer from Ethiopia’s northern and drought-prone Amhara region, relies on July rainfall for his teff, sorghum, maize, and wheat for bulgur. He also receives government-provided coffee, neem, and gesho seeds, but was unable to plant any crop until August, when the season’s first rains arrived.

“In previous years, September was a period when crops were already developing and food such as bulgur and maize were becoming available for consumption,” he said. “The delays affected the seedlings we plant, our crops, and the availability of animal feed.”

On Argane’s hillside in the Gurage Zone, however, signs of restoration are already visible. Since 2019, he has planted grass, fodder, fenugreek, and fruit trees along the edges of his fields, helping to hold soil in place while providing feed for the four cows, six goats, and three sheep that he keeps for milk and meat. His barley harvest has risen from about 1,800 pounds per acre to roughly 3,200, while the trees and grasses have reduced erosion and slowed the flow of water across his land during heavy rains.

“Restoring degraded land isn’t just about protecting the environment,” Argane said. “It’s also about making life better for my family and community.”

stories.summary: Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court and was remanded in custody.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 October 2026, 11:27 BST

The man accused of murdering the former MP Ann Widdecombe in July has appeared in court faced with a new allegation of preparing terrorist acts, including trying to break into the home of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said Joshua Kerry, 28, is alleged to have carried out online reconnaissance of "prominent people and institutions... including identifying the home address of Nigel Farage".

The prosecutor later told Westminster Magistrates' Court that damage was found on the doorframe at Farage's home address, adding: "the inference is that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house".

Kerry was accompanied by four custody officers in the dock and was remanded in custody to appear at the Old Bailey on Friday.

Kerry appeared in person the court. With a thick beard and wearing a grey sweatshirt and trousers, he spoke only to confirm his address in Rotherham and his date of birth.

He was told he faced a new charge of preparing terrorist acts between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026 by carrying out research on targets and travelling to, and attempting to gain entry to, the home of Nigel Farage.

The court heard that in April 2025 Nigel Farage's partner found that damage had been caused to their main front door at their house and a bottle of lighter fluid was found in the porch.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.

stories.title: Greens face conference centre ban over Zionism motion
stories.summary: Brighton & Hove City Council says the motion is not compatible with its inclusion commitments.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Green Party conference was held in October at the Brighton Centre

Published 4 hours ago

The Green Party of England and Wales could be barred from holding future conferences at the Brighton Centre after the party passed a motion declaring Zionism was racism .

The leader of Brighton & Hove City Council (BHCC), Labour's Bella Sankey, said she was "deeply concerned at the prospect of the Green Party returning to Brighton for future conferences".

She claimed the motion was "divisive, discriminatory and wrong" and was not compatible with Brighton & Hove's commitments to be a welcoming and inclusive city.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, said he would "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

Refusing future bookings

BHCC owns and operates the Brighton Centre, which has hosted party political conferences for decades.

Sankey told the BBC she was considering refusing to allow the Greens to hire the venue for future events.

In a statement, she claimed the motion had "dangerously" conflated the right of Jewish self-determination with the actions of the Israeli government and risked "the safety of Jewish members and Jewish people more broadly".

Sankey said people should never feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs

Zionism is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland.

Sankey went on to accuse the Green Party's leadership of a "dereliction of duty", adding "the Brighton Centre is owned by all of us in the city and should never be a place where people feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs".

Green Party sources have rejected Sankey's characterisation of the motion.

Polanski, who is Jewish, said that antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state "are, and must always be, completely distinct - blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe".

He added: "It's our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK."

The Brighton Centre was used by both the Greens and Liberal Democrats to host their autumn conferences this year.

The venue has also hosted Labour's annual gathering in previous years.

In 2017, the council's then-leader, Warren Morgan, who also represented Labour, threatened to ban his own party from holding its conference at the venue , external over concerns that anti-semitic views had been aired.

stories.title: The candidates hoping to be London's second Tory mayor
stories.summary: The Tory party has closed applications to be their candidate for mayor and there are four hopefuls.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
City Hall, the headquarters of the Greater London Authority

Published 7 October 2026, 06:14 BST

"We need to treat London seriously" - the words of a leading Conservative MP as his party considers its next candidate to be mayor of the capital.

The party has just closed applications for the role and there are four runners who have openly declared.

In 26 years, the Tories have only had one mayor in the capital, Boris Johnson, who won two elections and served from 2008 to 2016.

The party has lost three elections since then to Sadiq Khan, now Lord Khan of Tooting.

Gareth Bacon MP, shadow minister for London, told a meeting at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham this week that his party had treated the mayoralty like a "paper candidacy" in the past two elections - meaning that they hadn't taken it seriously enough.

Bacon said that the party had "cut Susan Hall adrift", a reference to their candidate in the last mayoral election in 2024, when Lord Khan won that historic third term as mayor.

Bacon went on to describe Lord Khan as "toxic and divisive".

Boris Johnson was the first - and so far only - Tory mayor of London

The election for mayor of London will be held in May 2028.

That is more than 18 months away, but the race is well under way.

Reform UK selected their candidate, Leila Cunningham, in January.

Sarah Olney, MP for Richmond Park, and Rob Blackie, who ran in 2024, are both candidates for the Lib Dem nomination.

This time round, with speculation about whether the current mayor will stand for a fourth term, the Conservatives sniff a chance.

On the back of local elections in May 2026 when the party won back traditional strongholds like Westminster and Wandsworth from Labour, they feel the mood may be changing.

However, winning the mayoralty may be too big a task. Much of it will depend on who they choose as their candidate.

So who's in the running?

Sir James Cleverly MP

Sir James Cleverly served as a government minister under several prime ministers

As the putative front runner, Braintree MP and former home secretary and foreign secretary James Cleverly has been working the conference circuit very hard.

Once a London Assembly member, and former head of the London Fire Authority, he is seen by many Tories as the 'shoo-in' candidate.

But he will come with baggage - he is a Brexiteer and when he was head of London's Fire Authority oversaw a big cuts programme.

He told me: "I hope to be a real champion for London, not just an administrator. I would make sure people are safe on the street and can really make a life for themselves and their families and can afford to live in London."

Cleverly said party political affiliations "are less important than someone with a real plan to make London a city we can be proud of again".

He added: "I hope to get the candidacy and then be a real champion for London, not just an administrator but a real champion and it's the city I love and that's why I want to put myself forward."

Festus Akinbusoye

Festus Akinbusoye is a former Bedfordshire police and crime commissioner

Festus Akinbusoye is a relative newcomer to London politics, though not to the city.

He emigrated from Nigeria with his parents and sister at age 13 in 1991 and lived in Canning Town in east London.

Akinbusoye was the Bedfordshire police and crime commissioner from 2021 to 2024 and was elected to Westminster City Council in May.

He told me: "We do not have to accept that this is the best we can get.

"I believe that we don't have to accept that just because we're a global city, London has got to be so unaffordable to build a life in.

"I want to be the most pro-policing, pro-house building, pro-business, pro-family, pro-growth mayor London has ever had.

"We can make that happen because London works when Londoners work".

Andrew Boff

Andrew Boff has been on the London Assembly since 2008

Andrew Boff is the current chair of the London Assembly.

Privately, Conservatives joke that it wouldn't be a mayoral selection without him in it. He's been an assembly member since 2008.

They also know he thinks very deeply about the capital's issues, particularly housing.

Why put his name forward again?

He told me: "I've got a very ambitious programme of not telling people how much I love London - because I'm hoping all the candidates love London - but specifically what I'm going to do.

"One of the things we've got to do is help the family housing crisis, so I will make sure we get more money for building those important family-sized homes.

"We need more encouragement for young people to do self-building in housing, so I'll be making land available for young people to build their own homes without having to pay for the cost of the land."

Boff added: "I'll get rid of the outward extension of the Ulez."

Alex Challoner

Alex Challoner said he has made his home in London for more than 30 years

Public affairs professional Alex Challoner told me he came to London from the West Country when he was 21 and has called the city his home for 35 years.

He said: "I think as a party, we have a choice between winning and losing for a fourth consecutive time.

"If we're serious about winning we have to have some of the boldest policies that will appeal to Londoners.

"I'm proposing a crackdown on fair dodgers at the Tube barriers by introducing British Transport Police, as well as training up Transport for London staff to stop people breaking through the barriers."

He told me his plan, called Fare Watch, would use a "simple reporting tool in the TfL Go app and online" where passengers will be able to report persistent fare dodging.

Challoner also pledged to introduce "a London Plan that you can read in an afternoon" as well as VAT cut "for gyms and London breweries".

The hopefuls in the race to be the Conservative mayoral candidate will have to wait until November to find out if they've made the final shortlist.

It is believed that London party members will then be offered a choice of two candidates.

I'm told the final two are likely to be announced on 20 November.

The original proposed date had been Friday the 13th, until it was pointed out that that may not be the most auspicious date to unveil candidates.

stories.title: Ex-Welsh Green Party deputy says Zionism motion 'pointless' after quitting party
stories.summary: Phil Davies called for Welsh Greens to set up their own party in the wake of the conference row.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Phil Davies was a youth activist and campaigner when he was chosen to be the Greens' deputy leader in Wales in 2024

Published 7 October 2026, 07:45 BST

The Green Party's former deputy leader in Wales says he resigned over the motion to declare "Zionism is racism" because it was "pointless" and some of the statements made were "disgraceful".

Phil Davies announced on social media on Tuesday his decision to quit the party had been "accelerated" by Sunday's conference motion.

In the post he had described the motion as "imperialistic" and "idiotic", and said Welsh Greens should consider splitting away from the English part of the party.

In response party leader Zack Polanski reissued a statement, originally sent on Monday , saying he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

The party leader, who is Jewish, added that "anti-semitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

What is Zionism? A very brief history

The motion, which was passed at a party conference to become party policy , called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Davies said he did not know why the motion was discussed "as it doesn't do anything to materially improve people's lives in Palestine".

He said Welsh Greens leader Anthony Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to quit, and also said he hoped Welsh party members would vote to split from those in England at a conference next month.

Welsh first minister says Green Party Zionist motion was ill-judged Published 18 hours ago

Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court Published 17 hours ago

Davies said it was "not the sort of politics" he wanted to be associated with, and that Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to leave the party.

He said: "Our views are exactly the same to be honest with you.

"He sent me a very nice message yesterday as well. I class Anthony as a close friend and that will remain."

When asked on whether Slaughter would follow him in quitting the party, Davies said he did not agree with any elected official resigning and staying in the Senedd.

"You weren't voted in as an individual member under this system. You're voted in under your party banner," he added.

He suggested that Welsh members of the party should consider splitting from the Green Party of England and Wales (GPEW) to "stand on our own two feet as a Welsh party" in light of the motion.

Davies said he was "hoping they'll vote to leave" at their party conference next month.

In an Instagram post, Davies said he had not been treated with respect or been "given enough support from the GPEW".

He added: "I have often felt like the token Welshman moaning at various points, but have not seen enough action taken by GPEW.

"I also feel the position of Wales deputy leaders is ignored rather than supported by GPEW."

Slaughter, who revealed he had been diagnosed with cancer last month, said his former colleague had brought a "much needed new perspective to Welsh politics".

He said: "I am positive he will contribute a great deal to Welsh public life whatever his next steps are.

"While the recent motion is not the only reason for Phil's resignation, I know it has stirred emotions across our party as people express their positions on this issue."

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said on Tuesday that the Green Party policy was "ill-judged" , saying that he had always advocated the two-state solution.

He had been responding to Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner, who had accused "left-wing parties" of having a "sickening antisemitism problem".

Speaking in the Senedd on Tuesday, ap Iorwerth said he always advocated the two-state solution and stood "shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish communities in Wales".

stories.title: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate
stories.summary: Israel has threatened to close the consulate, which handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city, over British sanctions on Israeli settlements.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 October 2026

The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.

Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.

The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.

The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.

UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.

According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.

Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme, former British ambassador to Israel, Matthew Gould, said any decision by the UK to expel Israeli diplomats would inflict "grievous damage" on the relationship between both countries.

He said areas affected could include defence, security and technology.

Gould told the programme: "When you've got to a stage where you are chucking out the big majority of Israeli diplomats in London, I don't think that's purely symbolic.

"I think at that point you're doing really quite serious damage to the structure and the substructure of the relationship."

He added that governments "have a choice", that the expulsion of Israeli diplomats would be a "gift to the Israeli right", and would help Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu win re-election.

France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.

Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."

She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close.

"It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

Watch: Kemi Badenoch says she wants Reform voters to "come back"

Published 6 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.

The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".

Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.

As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.

Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different from the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.

She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles , external .

Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.

She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win.

"The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority.

"My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."

A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election.

Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."

Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".

She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour . Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".

Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches .

Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received , including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.

Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down.

"That's what we're about."

Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.

Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.

Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election , arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.

Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party" .

This video can not be played

Young Tories asked if their party should do a deal with Reform UK

In her speech to the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, Badenoch is expected to say growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government" if her party wins power.

She will contrast her approach with that of Burnham's government, accusing Labour of "reckless" spending, adding billions to the national debt and increasing taxes.

Pitching the fight against Labour as "a battle for the soul of this nation", she will argue her party is "a renewed Conservative Party fighting again for the belief that what people earn belongs to them, not government".

Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24.

The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice.

The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year.

On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job".

She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today."

The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.

They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21.

The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training.

Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first.

"So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it.

"If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else."

A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training".

Watch: BBC sees police raid on fake gay asylum claims gang

Published 6 October 2026

Immigration enforcement have made arrests in connection with a suspected criminal network believed to be behind dozens of fake asylum claims from people pretending to be gay.

Those targeted by Home Office immigration enforcement officers on Tuesday morning are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence, including staged photographs and fake documents.

They are thought to have aided dozens of asylum claims from Bangladeshi men, claiming they would be in fear for their lives if they returned home.

Two people were arrested at addresses in London on Tuesday on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash.

A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally.

Three were arrested at addresses in London on Tuesday morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences

It follows a BBC investigation earlier this year , which revealed that law firms and advisers were helping migrants pose as gay in an effort to get asylum.

Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said Tuesday's arrests were over separate fake claims connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.

He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months.

"We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between £1,000 and £4,500," Foster said.

"It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."

More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.

Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.

The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.

The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.

A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.

In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.

She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.

Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."

The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims.

Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay.

Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection".

"To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said.

"And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."

A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

stories.body:
In the second article in a series on the Polish economy, we look at how the country is forging closer ties with its neighbours

T wo miles off the coast of Gdańsk, the white steel piles of Poland’s first offshore gas terminal rise from the slate-grey Baltic. Installed at a height eight metres above the waves, the floating cranes and construction vessels here are on the frontline of Europe’s push for energy security.

Since the taps were turned off on Russian gas after Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine four years ago, Poland has turned to the global energy market for supplies. But while conditions are far from ideal as the Middle East war drives oil and gas prices to stratospheric levels, strengthening the diversity of the country’s energy mix remains a top priority for Poland, its Baltic neighbours, and the EU at large.

Looking out to sea from the windswept beach backed by pine forest, Maciej Wawrzkowicz, the offshore project manager at the national gas company Gaz-System, and the construction manager Krzysztof Polatynski say the Baltic is not an easy place to build.

Before work could start, Polish navy minesweepers were called in to torpedo unexploded mines and bombs from the second world war. Construction is halted by storms, while the sea froze over last winter. But speed is important in this project of international significance.

“Every quay that’s available right now in the area that has some prefabrication workshop space, a contractor is occupying them. And you are seeking for more. Gdańsk harbour is a significant construction place right now.”

Poland used to import more than half of its gas from Russia but refused to pay in rubles in 2022 as the Kremlin became a pariah in the west over Putin’s war on Ukraine. A Norwegian pipeline under the Baltic and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Świnoujście, close to the border with Germany, helped to keep most homes warm and the fires of industry burning.

At Gdańsk the construction of the floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) – a specialised marine vessel used to store and convert LNG – is planned to further bolster Poland’s booming economy . But it will also increase the country’s capacity beyond domestic needs – turning it into a hub for eastern Europe and its Baltic neighbours.

Poland has LNG regasification capacity of 8.3bn cubic metres a year. Once the FRSU is operational in early 2028, that will add 6.1bn cubic metres a year of additional capacity. A second vessel at the Gdańsk FRSU is also planned for 2030 to lift total capacity to more than 20bn cubic metres a year.

In an age of geopolitical challenges, the FSRU vessel also has a symbolic name: “Solidarity”, in a nod to its home port’s history, and Poland’s drive to strengthen EU ties in the face of Russian aggression.

In the 1980s, as the Soviet Union crumbled, strikes at Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk over communist rule launched Poland’s Solidarność (Solidarity) movement. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it paved the way for independence and the transition to a free-market economy. Living standards have shot up since, from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.

Agnieszka Ozga, the director of the energy transition division, and her deputy, Paweł Sęk, say Poland has been working to diversify energy supplies for decades, with the 2014 annexation of Crimea by Russia accelerating the process. But 2022 was a “gamechanger,” says Sęk.

“After the war started, we knew what was going on and we knew many countries in our region would end up with no gas flows coming from Russia”.

Since then the Gdańsk FSRU has grown in importance, says Ozga. “Not only for Poland. But also Slovakia; central and eastern Europe countries; the Baltic states. It is also very, very important for the European Commission: to end the isolation of the Baltic states, because they were fully dependent on inflows of gas from Russia.”

However, there is also plenty of evidence in Gdańsk highlighting the energy challenges Poland must still confront.

On the edges of the old town’s narrow cobbled streets, the red and white-banded chimney stacks of a Soviet-era coal-fired power plant belch out thick plumes of smoke. Tourist boats ferrying visitors to the Westerplatte peninsula – where the first shots of the second world war were fired – must also pass through the jet-black mountains of a coal dock.

Coal accounts for more than half of electricity generation in Poland, significantly above the EU average. The legacy of Soviet fossil-fuel infrastructure and centuries of domestic production in this resource-rich country mean it remains key for the economy.

More than 80,000 people still work in coalmines , mainly in the south around the industrial city of Katowice – once called Stalinogród – as one of the few remaining coalmining regions still digging among EU countries fully committed to decarbonisation.

However, cutting out coal in favour of LNG, renewables and nuclear power is seen as critical for Poland’s future sovereignty and prosperity.

Relying on heavily polluting and costly fossil fuels, the country’s average wholesale electricity prices are the ninth highest in the EU – holding back growth in a country accustomed to powering ahead.

As wages and living standards catch up to western European levels, Polish manufacturing is beginning to lose its competitive edge from cheap labour – a factor that had long attracted multinationals such as Volkswagen and Toyota to locate factories in the country. As a result, keeping down other production costs – such as energy – is growing in importance.

after newsletter promotion

Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Krakow, is among Poland’s concerned entrepreneurs.

“The competitive cost of energy is not our big advantage. So we need to somehow change and reshape and focus on those elements of our economy that we can compete against, let’s say, France, that has the cheapest cost of energy. We cannot compete on the most cost-driven industries.”

Warsaw has pushed in recent years to decarbonise with a strategy up to 2040. However, critics warn that it still puts the country on a path to being the last EU economy to be producing the most of its power from fossil fuels by 2030 , endangering economic security and prosperity.

It will also require vast levels of public investment, at a time when the national debt is piling up and borrowing costs are rising. There are also political challenges in the run-up to a general election next year, with rightwing opponents of Donald Tusk’s liberal government pushing to rally Eurosceptic voters by weaponising the green transition.

The government is also investing in nuclear, building a plant on the Baltic coast. However, critics highlight an eye-watering price tag of more than €42bn (£35.6bn), for a facility that will not come online until the late 2030s.

Poland’s deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki says EU membership is, however, aiding a transition that will strengthen the economy. “We inherited from communist times the worst electricity or power mix of all EU members. It is changing – maybe not fast enough – but it is changing quite fast.”

Poland has secured €54.7bn in funding through the EU’s post-Covid recovery and resilience facility , with 40% going primarily to energy-related objectives. It is also the largest beneficiary of a Brussels fund intended to support the introduction of the EU’s emissions trading system carbon-pricing scheme.

“Poles are the world champions in getting EU funds,” Bosacki says. Since joining the bloc in 2004 he estimates more than €300bn has flowed to Warsaw, supporting road building, railways and other critical infrastructure to power its economic boom.

“We calculate the growth of Polish GDP would be half of what actually happened in the last 20 years if Poland was not a member of the EU. Almost a half.”

After annual output surpassed $1tn (£756bn) last year – ranking Poland as the sixth largest economy in the EU, ahead of countries including Belgium, Sweden and Austria – the flow of catchup funds from Brussels is, however, likely to dwindle.

Mateusz Urban, a Warsaw-based economist at Oxford Economics , says changing the energy system by 2040 will be tough. But ditching its status as a laggard in the green transition is vital – for the climate, for energy independence, and economic security.

In the past, Poland has come under pressure from the Kremlin using its gas supplies for political ends, including attempts in 2010 to extract punishing terms from Warsaw that would have stitched up the Polish gas market in Russia’s favour.

“If you have one big supplier through a pipeline you have no power,” Urban says.

With the closure of the strait of Hormuz and as Donald Trump rattles the global energy market by threatening to limit diesel exports, risks remain. Large volumes of the LNG imported by sea to Poland are from the US and Qatar. But Polish energy officials are sanguine, suggesting that other markets could still be utilised, and argue widening horizons beyond Russian imports remains critical.

Urban agrees that diversifying energy supplies, while renewable power generation takes time to develop, could help strengthen Poland’s hand.

“We need it for geopolitical security. Moving away from Russian gas, and coal, is a huge step forward. If you have a diverse supply, then you’re more insulated from trouble in each region.”

stories.title: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies
stories.summary: The government and the Conservatives both agree the UK needs better air defences in an increasingly dangerous world.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Current air-defence systems include the Sky Sabre but defence chiefs have warned more is needed

Published 6 October 2026

America and Israel's war with Iran has shown that even the world's most sophisticated air defences can be overwhelmed by enemy missiles and drones, if fired in significant numbers.

Iran's have broken through the layered air defences of US military bases in the Middle-East causing significant damage.

Russia's war in Ukraine has also exposed the huge challenge of defending their own skies from large-scale attacks.

The government's Strategic Defence Review, published in 2025, explicitly warned of the threats to the UK – including ballistic and cruise missiles and drones – and highlighted the need for the UK to invest more in its air defences.

The Labour government is allocating up to £1bn to address it.

The Conservatives now say they will spend more - £10 bn - over a decade. Both parties agree that the UK needs layers of air defences.

Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system Published 1 day ago

Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still lack a weapons system to deal with long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles.

And those don't come cheap. Each interceptor used by the US Patriot missile system costs about $4m (£3m).

Sophisticated air defences that can deal with a range of threats are expensive. The US Army alone wants to increase its budget for both missiles and interceptors by fourfold next year – to $36bn (£27.1bn).

Israel also spends a significant proportion of its $45bn (£33.9bn) annual military budget on air defences.

For the Conservatives there's also a presentation problem. Their original press release mentioned building a new air defence systems that would be "in essence, a British Iron Dome", referencing Israel's elaborate air defence system .

But any comparison of the challenge of defending Britain's skies with Israel's, about 10% the size of the UK, is naive.

Nor is the threat the same. Israel has regularly been targeted by drones and missiles over the past decade. The UK has not.

The Conservatives now suggest the phrase "Iron Dome" was just a shorthand for better air defences. But even the words "Britannia Shield" may be a misnomer.

It would be nigh on impossible for the UK to develop an air-defence system that could defend the whole country with such limited resources.

At best it could afford a system to protect some key strategic sites – including military bases. At present the UK doesn't even have that.

How much money are other countries spending on air defences?

By BBC Verify

Nick Fiorenza, a defence analyst from Janes, a military intelligence company, said the money committed by the government to missile defence under the Defence Investment Plan "is only a fraction of what other countries have declared".

He said the Conservatives' plan to invest £10bn "sounds comparable to what other small countries are doing".

He continued: "Not as small as the Netherlands or Belgium, but let's say Germany or Turkey and now the Greeks are working on something called Achilles Shield.

"That's the kind of magnitude [spending £10bn] that would be required for a serious missile defence system."

Germany is leading the European Sky Shield Initiative (ESSI), a 24‑nation effort to jointly procure air and missile defence systems (IRIS‑T, Patriot, Arrow 3).

Berlin has committed roughly €4bn (£3.4bn) for Arrow 3 alone and is also part of a €5.1bn (£4.3bn) plan to share up to 1,000 Patriot GEM‑T interceptors with Romania, Spain and the Netherlands.

In France, budgets show an "Air and Air Defence" spend of about €4.4bn (£3.7bn) in 2026, but this covers all air force air defence activities, not just missile defence.

Poland, which spends more on defence as a share of its economy than the UK, is building an air and missile defence system worth more than PLN 200bn (£39bn) which will be spent over a number of years.
